claim: The Decimate modifier reduces a mesh's face count by a ratio while attempting to preserve overall silhouette and major features -- shown converting a dense sculpted mesh (thousands of quads) into a much lower-poly version that still reads recognizably as the same form. Conceptual purpose: converting dense sculpts/scans into lightweight assets for real-time or distant-background use, not a precision topology tool (it does not produce clean quad flow, just fewer polygons).
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched full video; source video is older than the current Blender version, so treated as conceptual overview only, not current UI/parameter truth): at 1:31, a dense Suzanne mesh is reduced via Decimate's ratio slider into a much lower-poly version while preserving general silhouette and features.

claim: The Remesh modifier rebuilds a mesh's entire topology into a uniform grid (historically voxel-based) regardless of the input's original topology quality -- shown converting messy, stretched n-gon topology (from extruded text) into an evenly-spaced uniform quad grid. Conceptual purpose: recovering a workable topology from geometry with genuinely bad/chaotic input topology (extruded text, CAD imports, boolean-mangled meshes) as a base for sculpting or further work, at the cost of discarding the original edge flow entirely.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 2:47, an extruded text letter with messy, stretched n-gon topology is converted via Remesh into a uniform, evenly-spaced quad grid across the whole surface.
rejected_alternative: Manually retopologizing messy CAD/text/boolean-mangled geometry by hand
reason: Remesh discards the original topology entirely in favor of a uniform grid, trading edge-flow control for a fast, workable starting point on geometry whose original topology isn't worth preserving anyway.

claim: The Curve modifier conforms a straight mesh (e.g. a repeating chain of blocks or a tube) to follow the exact path of an assigned curve/spline object -- shown bending a rigid straight chain of blocks into an S-curve matching a spline's shape. Conceptual purpose: distinct from the Screw modifier (revolves a profile around an axis) -- this bends existing straight geometry along an arbitrary path, the go-to technique for cables, ropes, tank treads, train tracks, belts, and other segmented objects that need to flow along a designed curve rather than a simple revolve.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 4:33, a straight, rigid chain of repeating blocks is assigned a Curve modifier targeting a spline path and bends to follow the spline's exact S-curve shape in 3D space.
rejected_alternative: Manually rotating/positioning each segment of a chain to approximate a curved path

claim: Beyond its use as a broad-blockout tool on a mesh BEFORE fine detail exists (already captured from RileyB3D's build), a Lattice modifier is equally applicable to reshaping an ALREADY-DETAILED, dense mesh -- shown globally bending/tapering a cylindrical object covered in hundreds of fine window-like cutouts by moving just a handful of lattice control points, without individually touching any of the fine surface detail.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 5:15, a low-resolution lattice cage placed around a dense cylindrical mesh with hundreds of fine cutout details bends and tapers the whole form via a few lattice control points, without disturbing the fine surface detail.
rejected_alternative: Manually moving thousands of individual vertices to reshape an already-detailed dense mesh
reason: This generalizes the earlier-captured Lattice principle (useful for broad blockout before detail exists) to a second, equally valid use case: reshaping a mesh that already has fine detail, which manual vertex-by-vertex editing cannot do without disturbing that detail.
